content: Corns and calluses are areas of thickened skin that develop as a result of repeated pressure or friction. These are not serious medical conditions but can cause discomfort or pain in some cases. Symptoms of Corns and Calluses: The skin becomes thickened and hardened. The affected areas may appear flaky and dry. Hardened, thickened skin is commonly found on the hands, feet, or other areas subjected to frequent rubbing or pressure. Causes of Corns and Calluses: Corns and calluses are caused by persistent pressure or friction on the skin. Corns typically form on the top or sides of toes, often due to ill-fitting shoes. Calluses usually develop on the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet. The thickening of the skin is a natural protective response to prevent injury, such as blisters. For example, farmers and rowers often develop calluses on their hands to protect against painful blisters. Individuals with bunions may develop calluses over the bunion due to constant rubbing against footwear. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider can diagnose corns and calluses by visually examining the affected skin. In most cases, no additional tests are required. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: If you have diabetes or experience numbness in your feet or toes, it is crucial to regularly inspect your feet for any issues. If you have diabetes and notice any foot problems, contact your healthcare provider immediately. For most individuals, switching to properly fitting shoes or wearing gloves during activities that cause friction can resolve the issue. If a corn or callus appears infected or does not improve with treatment, consult your healthcare provider. Seek medical attention if you experience persistent symptoms such as pain, redness, warmth, or drainage from the affected area. Treatment Options: Preventing friction is usually the primary treatment for corns and calluses. If a corn is caused by poorly fitting shoes, switching to properly fitting footwear can resolve the issue within a few weeks. In the meantime, protect the affected area with donut-shaped corn pads, which are available at pharmacies. A pumice stone can be used to gently reduce the thickness of the corn if desired. Calluses on the hands can be managed by wearing gloves during activities that cause friction, such as gardening or weightlifting. If an infection or ulcer develops in the area of a corn or callus, a healthcare provider may need to remove unhealthy tissue, and antibiotics may be required. Calluses often indicate excessive pressure on the skin due to an underlying condition, such as bunions. Addressing the underlying issue can prevent the recurrence of calluses. Prognosis: Corns and calluses are rarely serious and, with proper treatment, typically improve without causing long-term complications. Possible Complications: Complications from corns and calluses are uncommon. Individuals with diabetes are at higher risk of developing ulcers and infections. They should regularly examine their feet to detect any problems early. Any foot injuries in people with diabetes require prompt medical attention.
